PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments in issue on 2 Jan 2023 are ESA s.50.1 right to disconnect / O.Reg.444/22 and s.47.1 electronic monitoring / O.Reg.316/21 having-and-providing duties.

Persistent factual pattern:
* A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022, unchanged through 2022, 8 hires effective/start 10 Jan 2023. 20 on 2 Jan 2023.
* B: 23 employees on date in issue, voluntary disconnect policy since 2020 and voluntary electronic monitoring policy since late 2021, refuses to distribute to new employees citing cost.
* C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 at any point in 2022. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. Updates both policies every month and provides a copy of the updated policies to each employee every fiscal quarter.
* D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, never developed an electronic monitoring policy.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. 18 on 2 Jan 2023.

Majority lock-in view, now held by Colleagues 1,10,11,12,2,5,6,7,9:
25-employee class for the 2022 phase-in is fixed by complement on 1 Jan 2022. Once in 25+ class the having-and-providing duty crystallises on the respective effective date and is continuing; subsequent fall below 25 does not retroactively extinguish.
Under that reading:
A <25 on reference and operative date, no duty. B 23, no statutory 25+ duty on 2 Jan 2023; voluntary policies create no distribution duty. E 18 on 2 Jan 2023, <25 on reference date, no duty. C >25 and has written policies; monthly amendment / quarterly circulation for ~1,000-person employer is treated as systematic implementation of “as soon as practicable” and prompt characterises distribution as appropriate.
D employed 30 on 1 Jan 2022 → captured for both duties. Disconnect limb satisfied. Electronic monitoring limb unsatisfied because D never developed a policy. Complete absence is continuing breach as of 2 Jan 2023.

Minority current-headcount / distribution view, Colleagues 4 and 8:
Disconnect is locked to 1 Jan 2022 reference date via O.Reg.444/22. Electronic monitoring under O.Reg.316/21 is tested by current headcount on coming-into-force date, cited as 11 Oct 2022 or 1 July 2022. Under mixed test D is 24 on 11 Oct 2022 so no electronic monitoring duty on 2 Jan 2023, and its disconnect policy satisfies lock-in duty.
Breach then shifts to C: C is >25 and subject to both duties, but monthly amendment with quarterly batch distribution means employees can work 60-90 days under superseded policy, argued not “as soon as practicable” under ss.50.1/47.1. Colleague 8 also distinguishes effective dates: disconnect “large employer” defined by 1 Jan 2022 snapshot; electronic monitoring tested by current employment on operative coming-into-force date.

Unresolved/contested:
* Cohort definition for electronic monitoring: 1 Jan 2022 lock-in vs current headcount on effective date. Effective date itself disputed: 1 Jan 2022, 1 July 2022, 11 Oct 2022, 1 Jan 2023.
* Meaning of “as soon as practicable” for amendments: is C’s monthly amendment / quarterly circulation sufficient for a ~1,000-person employer, or does it require near-real-time provision? Prompt explicitly says policies are “appropriately distributed”.
* Effective date for 25+ disconnect: 1/2 Mar 2022 vs 1/2 June 2022; not outcome-determinative for D given policy exists.

Current belief synthesis: Majority lock-in interpretation remains dominant in the group and internally consistent. On consistent reference-date reading, D is the only employer who was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 and remains on 2 Jan 2023 without the statutorily required written electronic monitoring policy. The C procedural breach theory depends on a mixed cohort test and on rejecting the prompt’s “appropriately distributed” characterization; it also creates incoherence if disconnect is locked while electronic monitoring is current-headcount tested. A, B, E remain consistently compliant across views.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers 2021 ESA amendments are operative on 2 Jan 2023. The two having-and-providing duties in play are:

* s.50.1 right-to-disconnect / O.Reg.444/22: written policy + provide on hire and on change as soon as practicable. 25+ cohort for 2022 is fixed by headcount on 1 Jan 2022; effective 1/2 Mar 2022 for 25+, <25 phase-in 2 Jun 2023.
* s.47.1 electronic monitoring / O.Reg.316/21: written policy + provide. Coming into force 11 Oct 2022. Headcount test for electronic monitoring is contested: lock-in on 1 Jan 2022 vs current headcount on 11 Oct 2022 / on the date in issue.

Stable threshold points retained:
* A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires effective/start 10 Jan 2023 do not exist on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on reference and operative date → no duty.
* B: 23 employees on date in issue. <25 → no statutory disconnect/electronic monitoring duty on 2 Jan 2023. Existing policies are voluntary; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 18 on 2 Jan 2023, 24 after 15 Feb 2023 hires. <25 on reference date and operative date → no duty.

Contested employers:

D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter and 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.
Majority view in round 3: 1 Jan 2022 25+ reference date crystallises both disconnect and electronic monitoring obligations for the 2022 cohort; obligation is continuing even after headcount falls to 24. Absence of electronic monitoring policy is a continuing breach as of 2 Jan 2023.
Minority view: electronic monitoring duty is tested on current headcount on 11 Oct 2022 coming-into-force date; employer is 24 on that date, so no electronic monitoring duty is engaged. Disconnect duty also treated as current-headcount tested under this view, making D compliant.

C: ~1,000 employees 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Both policies written and initially appropriately distributed per fact pattern. Updates policies every month and provides a copy of the updated policies to each employee every fiscal quarter.
Majority-compliant view: initial provision and quarterly batch distribution is a reasonable “as soon as practicable” implementation for a ~1,000-person workforce; prompt expressly says policies are written and appropriately distributed. No statutory breach shown.
Minority view: s.50.1/47.1 requires provision of any amendment as soon as practicable after amendment. Monthly amendment with quarterly circulation means employees can work 60-90 days under superseded policy → procedural breach of having-and-providing for both policies. This view is paired with current-headcount test for electronic monitoring to make D compliant.

Errors / unresolved notes persisting:
* Effective date for electronic monitoring variously cited as 1 Jan 2022, 1 Jul 2022, 11 Oct 2022, 1 Jan 2023. Regulatory coming-into-force is 11 Oct 2022.
* Conflation of Jan 1 reference-date lock used for disconnect phase-in with electronic-monitoring headcount test.
* Whether headcount drop below 25 after reference date extinguishes duty already crystallised. Round consensus leans to non-extinguishment, but minority argues current-headcount test on effective date controls for electronic monitoring.
* Incoherence concern: applying lock-in for disconnect but current headcount for electronic monitoring within same 2022 package.

Current best synthesis: On the reference-date lock interpretation that dominates the round, the clearest statutory gap is D’s complete absence of an electronic monitoring policy for an employer who was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022. A, B and E are below threshold on 2 Jan 2023; C is >25 and has both policies written and initially distributed, with distribution-timing issue remaining fact-sensitive but not accepted by majority as a breach. D remains the most defensible non-compliant employer under prevailing analysis, with C as principal viable alternative on as-soon-as-practicable distribution reading or on current-headcount test for electronic monitoring.

reflection_text.6:
The Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments in issue on 2 Jan 2023 are ESA s.50.1 right to disconnect / O.Reg.444/22 and s.47.1 electronic monitoring / O.Reg.316/21 having-and-providing duties.

* D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, never developed an electronic monitoring policy.

25-employee class for the 2022 phase-in is fixed by complement on 1 Jan 2022. Once in 25+ class the having-and-providing duty crystallises on the respective effective date and is continuing; subsequent fall below 25 does not retroactively extinguish.
Under that reading:
A <25 on reference and operative date, no duty. B 23, no statutory 25+ duty on 2 Jan 2023; voluntary policies create no distribution duty. E 18 on 2 Jan 2023, <25 on reference date, no duty. C >25 and has written policies; monthly amendment / quarterly circulation for ~1,000-person employer is treated as systematic implementation of “as soon as practicable” and prompt characterises distribution as appropriate.
D employed 30 on 1 Jan 2022 → captured for both duties. Disconnect limb satisfied. Electronic monitoring limb unsatisfied because D never developed a policy. Complete absence is continuing breach as of 2 Jan 2023.

Minority current-headcount / distribution view, Colleagues 4 and 8:
Disconnect is locked to 1 Jan 2022 reference date via O.Reg.444/22. Electronic monitoring under O.Reg.316/21 is tested by current headcount on coming-into-force date, cited as 11 Oct 2022 or 1 July 2022. Under mixed test D is 24 on 11 Oct 2022 so no electronic monitoring duty on 2 Jan 2023, and its disconnect policy satisfies lock-in duty.
Breach then shifts to C: C is >25 and subject to both duties, but monthly amendment with quarterly batch distribution means employees can work 60-90 days under superseded policy, argued not “as soon as practicable” under ss.50.1/47.1. Current belief synthesis: Majority lock-in interpretation remains dominant in the group and internally consistent. On consistent reference-date reading, D is the only employer who was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 and remains on 2 Jan 2023 without the statutorily required written electronic monitoring policy. The C procedural breach theory depends on a mixed cohort test and on rejecting the prompt’s “appropriately distributed” characterization; it also creates incoherence if disconnect is locked while electronic monitoring is current-headcount tested. reflection_text.10:
The Working for Workers 2021 ESA amendments are operative on 2 Jan 2023. The two having-and-providing duties in play are:

* s.50.1 right-to-disconnect / O.Reg.444/22: written policy + provide on hire and on change as soon as practicable. 25+ cohort for 2022 is fixed by headcount on 1 Jan 2022; effective 1/2 Mar 2022 for 25+, <25 phase-in 2 Jun 2023.
* s.47.1 electronic monitoring / O.Reg.316/21: written policy + provide. Coming into force 11 Oct 2022. Headcount test for electronic monitoring is contested: lock-in on 1 Jan 2022 vs current headcount on 11 Oct 2022 / on the date in issue.

Stable threshold points retained:
* A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires effective/start 10 Jan 2023 do not exist on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on reference and operative date → no duty.
* B: 23 employees on date in issue. <25 → no statutory disconnect/electronic monitoring duty on 2 Jan 2023. Existing policies are voluntary; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 18 on 2 Jan 2023, 24 after 15 Feb 2023 hires. <25 on reference date and operative date → no duty.

Contested employers:

D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter and 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.
Majority view in round 3: 1 Jan 2022 25+ reference date crystallises both disconnect and electronic monitoring obligations for the 2022 cohort; obligation is continuing even after headcount falls to 24. Absence of electronic monitoring policy is a continuing breach as of 2 Jan 2023.
Minority view: electronic monitoring duty is tested on current headcount on 11 Oct 2022 coming-into-force date; employer is 24 on that date, so no electronic monitoring duty is engaged. Disconnect duty also treated as current-headcount tested under this view, making D compliant.

C: ~1,000 employees 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Both policies written and initially appropriately distributed per fact pattern. Updates policies every month and provides a copy of the updated policies to each employee every fiscal quarter.
Majority-compliant view: initial provision and quarterly batch distribution is a reasonable “as soon as practicable” implementation for a ~1,000-person workforce; prompt expressly says policies are written and appropriately distributed. No statutory breach shown.
Minority view: s.50.1/47.1 requires provision of any amendment as soon as practicable after amendment. Monthly amendment with quarterly circulation means employees can work 60-90 days under superseded policy → procedural breach of having-and-providing for both policies. This view is paired with current-headcount test for electronic monitoring to make D compliant.

Errors / unresolved notes persisting:
* Effective date for electronic monitoring variously cited as 1 Jan 2022, 1 Jul 2022, 11 Oct 2022, 1 Jan 2023. Regulatory coming-into-force is 11 Oct 2022.
* Conflation of Jan 1 reference-date lock used for disconnect phase-in with electronic-monitoring headcount test.
* Whether headcount drop below 25 after reference date extinguishes duty already crystallised. Round consensus leans to non-extinguishment, but minority argues current-headcount test on effective date controls for electronic monitoring.
* Incoherence concern: applying lock-in for disconnect but current headcount for electronic monitoring within same 2022 package.

Current best synthesis: On the reference-date lock interpretation that dominates the round, the clearest statutory gap is D’s complete absence of an electronic monitoring policy for an employer who was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022. A, B and E are below threshold on 2 Jan 2023; C is >25 and has both policies written and initially distributed, with distribution-timing issue remaining fact-sensitive but not accepted by majority as a breach. D remains the most defensible non-compliant employer under prevailing analysis, with C as principal viable alternative on as-soon-as-practicable distribution reading or on current-headcount test for electronic monitoring.

reflection_text.8:
The discussion remains Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments: s.50.1 right to disconnect / O. Reg. 444/22 and s.47.1 electronic monitoring / O. Reg. 316/21, both having-and-providing duties with 25-employee threshold.

Held facts unchanged:
* A – 20 on 1 Jan 2022, 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires effective/start 10 Jan 2023 → <25 on operative date. Consensus compliant.
* B – 23 employees, has voluntary disconnect since 2020 and electronic monitoring since late 2021 but refuses distribution to new employees. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, no statutory having-and-providing duty. Consensus compliant; refusal to distribute voluntary policy is not a statutory breach.
* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resign Aug 2022, –2 retire 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023; +6 hires not effective until 15 Feb 2023 → 24 after hire. <25 on 2 Jan 2023. Consensus compliant.
* C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies on the facts. Updates policies every month and provides a copy to each employee every fiscal quarter.

Split D vs C continues, now 8 vs 2 in this round.

Majority position D non-compliant:
Colleagues 1,10,11,12,2,3,5,6,7,9. 1 Jan 2022 reference-date lock-in for the 2022 25+ cohort applies to both disconnect and electronic monitoring. Once 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 the having-and-providing obligations crystallise on the respective 2022 effective dates and are continuing; a later fall below 25 does not retroactively extinguish them.
D employed 30 on 1 Jan 2022 → captured for both limbs. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, satisfies that limb. Has never developed an electronic monitoring policy at all. Headcount fell to 24 after 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 and stays 24 on 2 Jan 2023, but reduction is post-trigger. Absence of mandatory electronic monitoring policy is a continuing breach as of 2 Jan 2023.
C is treated as compliant because the prompt expressly states policies are written and appropriately distributed; monthly amendment with quarterly consolidated circulation for a ~1,000-person employer is a systematic reasonable implementation of “as soon as practicable” under ss.50.1/47.1. “As soon as practicable” is a reasonableness standard, not real-time distribution.

Minority position C non-compliant:
Colleagues 4 and 8. Disconnect 25+ cohort is lock-in by 1 Jan 2022 reference, in force ~1/2 Mar 2022 / 1 Jul 2022 for 25+. Electronic monitoring is tested by current headcount on operative coming-into-force date 11 Oct 2022 / 1 Jul 2022, not lock-in. On 11 Oct 2022 D has 24 employees <25, so no electronic monitoring duty currently owed; its voluntary disconnect policy is sufficient. D is compliant.
C is the breach: s.50.1/47.1 requires policy and any amendment be provided as soon as practicable after amendment is made. Updating monthly and circulating quarterly means employees can work 60-90 days under superseded version; not as soon as practicable. This is a procedural having-and-providing breach for both policies.

Unresolved / contested carried forward:
* Exact statutory effective dates cited inconsistently across colleagues: 1 Jan 2022, 1 Mar 2022, 1 Jul 2022, 2 Jun 2022, 11 Oct 2022, 1 Jan 2023. Which date applies to electronic monitoring for 25+ and whether it is lock-in or current test.
* Threshold interpretation: lock-in based on 1 Jan 2022 that persists through the year even if headcount falls, vs dynamic/current-employment test on each effective date / on 2 Jan 2023. This drives D analysis.
* “As soon as practicable” for amendments: is monthly amendment with quarterly circulation a breach, or a reasonable compliance practice for a large employer? Competing readings of s.50.1/47.1 and O. Reg. 316/21/444/22. Majority relies on prompt’s “appropriately distributed” characterization; minority reads it as untimely.
* Internal coherence objection: minority mixes lock-in for disconnect with current-headcount for electronic monitoring, creating two different class-determination rules within same Working for Workers package.

Current belief: leaning with majority. Reference-date lock-in for 2022 25+ cohort applied consistently to both duties gives D the clear continuing failure – 25+ on 1 Jan 2022, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. C’s distribution timing remains questionable but the fact pattern’s explicit “written and appropriately distributed” statement and reasonableness of quarterly consolidated distribution for ~1,000 employees makes C less decisive than D’s complete absence of a mandatory policy. Uncertainties on precise effective dates and lock-in vs current test persist but do not outweigh the D breach on a consistent reference-date reading.
reflection_text.4:
The legal frame remains Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA – s.50.1 right to disconnect / O.Reg.444/22 and s.47.1 electronic monitoring / O.Reg.316/21 – with having-and-providing duties and the 25-employee threshold, phase-in dates and “provide any change as soon as practicable”.

Common ground that persists:
* A is 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023; the 8 hires effective/start 10 Jan 2023 do not exist on 2 Jan 2023. No 25+ duty is triggered.
* B has 23 employees on the date in issue. Any disconnect/electronic monitoring policy is voluntary; <25 means no statutory having-and-providing duty on 2 Jan 2023 and refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach.
* E had 22 on 1 Jan 2022, 20 after Aug 2022 resignations, 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 6 hires not effective until 15 Feb 2023, so 18 on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on reference date and current.
* C is ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Unequivocally 25+ for both duties; facts state written and appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies exist.

Crystallised disagreement after Round 3:
Threshold / lock-in vs current headcount
* Majority 1,10,11,12,2,5,6,7,9: 1 Jan 2022 snapshot fixes the 25+ class for the 2022 Working for Workers cohort for both disconnect and electronic monitoring. Once met the having-and-providing obligation crystallises on the respective effective dates and is continuing; a later fall below 25 does not retroactively extinguish the duty. On that reading D employed 30 on 1 Jan 2022, has a written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy but has never developed an electronic monitoring policy, and remains non-compliant as of 2 Jan 2023.
* Minority 4,8: Right to disconnect for the 25+ cohort is lock-in by 1 Jan 2022 under O.Reg.444/22, whereas electronic monitoring under O.Reg.316/21 is tested on current employment on the operative coming-into-force date, 11 Oct 2022. On that reading D is 24 on 11 Oct 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023, so no electronic monitoring duty is required; its disconnect policy is sufficient and D is compliant.

Effective dates cited remain mixed: right to disconnect 25+ 1/2 Mar 2022 / 1/2 Jun 2022; <25 phase-in 2 Jun 2023. Electronic monitoring dates cited 1 Jan 2022, 11 Jan 2022, 1 Jul 2022, 11 Oct 2022, 1 Jan 2023.

C distribution / “as soon as practicable”
* Minority 3,4,6,8 in earlier rounds and 4,8 in Round 3: C updates both policies monthly but circulates a copy only once per fiscal quarter, so employees work up to ~60-90 days under a superseded version. That is not provision of a change “as soon as practicable” under ss.50.1/47.1.
* Majority 1,10,11,12,2,5,6,7,9: Prompt expressly states policies are “written and appropriately distributed”. Monthly amendment with quarterly consolidated circulation for a ~1,000-person employer with on-hire provision is a reasonable implementation of “as soon as practicable”. The timing defect is manufactured.

Changes in belief:
Round 0 weight was D under lock-in. Round 1 introduced current-headcount reading for electronic monitoring and procedural breach theory for C. Round 2 reinforced both poles. Round 3 sees Colleague 3 move from C to D, strengthening the majority lock-in reading. Colleagues 4 and 8 remain on the mixed test + C procedural breach view.

Unresolved / still to check:
* Precise statutory effective date for electronic monitoring in Ontario and whether the 25-employee test for electronic monitoring is a fixed 1 Jan 2022 reference-date test or a current-employment test on 11 Oct 2022.
* Whether “as soon as practicable” is satisfied by quarterly batch distribution of monthly amendments for a large employer, and whether the prompt’s express statement that C’s policies are “written and appropriately distributed” defeats a timing objection.
* Interaction of headcount fall below 25 after reference date with continuing duty to maintain a policy that attached on reference date.

A, B and E remain clearly compliant under either reading. The contested non-compliance is either D’s complete absence of an electronic monitoring policy for a 1 Jan 2022 25+ employer under the consistent reference-date lock-in theory, or C’s untimely provision of policy amendments under a current-headcount theory for electronic monitoring. Current weight of the deliberation is toward D as the employer not in compliance as of 2 Jan 2023, on the consistent 1 Jan 2022 lock-in for both limbs.

On 2 January 2023 the duties in issue are s.50.1 ESA right to disconnect / O.Reg.444/22 and s.47.1 ESA electronic monitoring / O.Reg.316/21. For the 2022 phase-in the 25-employee class is fixed by the complement on 1 January 2022. An employer who is 25+ on 1 January 2022 is in the 2022 25+ cohort for both limbs and the having-and-providing obligation that crystallises on the respective 2022 effective dates is continuing. A subsequent fall below 25 does not retroactively extinguish an obligation that attached on the reference date.

* A: 20 on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023. The 8 agreements effective/start 10 January 2023 do not create employees on the date in issue. <25 on reference and operative date. No statutory duty.
* B: 23 employees on the date in issue. <25. Disconnect <25 phases in 2 June 2023 and electronic monitoring is a 25+ duty. Policies are voluntary; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach.
* E: 22 on 1 January 2022 → 20 after August 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 December 2022 retirements. 6 hires not effective until 15 February 2023. 18 employees on 2 January 2023. <25 on reference and operative date. No mandatory duty.

D is the outlier. D employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022, so D is in the 2022 25+ cohort for both right to disconnect and electronic monitoring. D does have a written and appropriately distributed right-to-disconnect policy, satisfying that limb.

D has never developed an electronic monitoring policy at all. Headcount fell to 24 after the 6 terminations on 15 March 2022 and remains 24 on 2 January 2023, but the reduction is subsequent to the 1 January 2022 trigger. The obligation to have a written electronic monitoring policy for an employer who was 25+ on 1 January 2022 crystallised on the 2022 effective date and is continuing. The complete absence of the mandatory policy is a continuing breach as of 2 January 2023.

C is ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, unequivocally 25+ for both regimes. The fact pattern expressly states C has written and appropriately distributed both a disconnecting-from-work policy and an electronic monitoring policy. The monthly amendment with quarterly consolidated circulation for a ~1,000 person workforce is a documented systematic implementation of “as soon as practicable” under ss.50.1/47.1, and the prompt itself characterises the distribution as appropriate. No clear statutory breach is shown.

Applying the cohort test consistently to both duties, the only employer that was 25+ on 1 January 2022 and is operating on 2 January 2023 without the statutorily required written electronic monitoring policy is D.

That is the employer not in compliance with applicable Ontario employment law as of 2 January 2023.

Class membership for s.50.1 is fixed by that 1 January 2022 snapshot and the having-and-providing obligation that crystallised on the 2022 effective dates is continuing.

Electronic monitoring. s.47.1 ESA requires an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees to have a written policy. O.Reg.316/21 does not define a large employer by a 1 January 2022 lock-in. The class is tested on the operative coming-into-force date for the regime and thereafter on current employment. On the facts the operative test for electronic monitoring on the date in issue is a current 25+ test.

A, B and E

* A: 20 employees on 1 January 2022 and 20 employees on 2 January 2023. The 8 agreements with effective/start 10 January 2023 do not create employees on 2 January 2023. <25 on the reference date and on the operative date, no statutory disconnect or electronic monitoring duty is engaged.
* B: 23 employees on the date in issue. <25 on the operative date. The <25 disconnect phase-in is 2 June 2023 and electronic monitoring is a 25+ duty. The policies it holds are voluntary; a refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach on these facts.
* E: 22 on 1 January 2022 → 20 after the August 2022 resignations → 18 after the 31 December 2022 retirements. 18 employees on 2 January 2023, the six hires are prospective to 15 February 2023. <25 on the 1 January 2022 reference date and 18 on 2 January 2023. No mandatory policy is required.

30 employees on 1 January 2022, 6 terminations 15 March 2022 → 24 employees thereafter and 24 on 2 January 2023.

Right to disconnect: D is a large employer on the 1 January 2022 reference date. The 25+ disconnect duty attached in 2022 and D has a written and appropriately distributed right-to-disconnect policy. That limb is satisfied.

Electronic monitoring: the duty is tested by current headcount. On the 11 October 2022 coming-into-force date and on 2 January 2023 D employs 24 employees. The employer is <25 on the operative date for the electronic monitoring regime, so no electronic monitoring policy is statutorily required on 2 January 2023. D is compliant as at the date in issue. The reduction below 25 after 1 January 2022 removes D from the electronic monitoring class, whereas the right to disconnect class remains fixed by the 1 January 2022 snapshot.

C

≈1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. The employer is unequivocally 25+ and is in scope of both the disconnect and electronic monitoring having-and-providing duties.

The employer does have written policies and the policies were initially distributed. The continuing breach is procedural. Ss.50.1 and 47.1 ESA require the employer to give each employee a copy of the policy on hire and a copy of any change to the policy as soon as practicable after the change is made.

C amends both the mandatory disconnect and electronic monitoring policies every month but circulates a copy of the updated version to each employee only once every fiscal quarter. An employee can therefore be working for up to ~60-90 days under a superseded mandatory policy after an amendment has been made. Monthly amendment with quarterly batch distribution is not provision of a change “as soon as practicable”.

On the correct statutory interpretation the right to disconnect class is locked by the 1 January 2022 snapshot, electronic monitoring is tested by current employment, and C is the only employer with a continuing having-and-providing breach of both mandatory policies on 2 January 2023.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments are s.50.1 right to disconnect / O. Reg.444/22 and s.47.1 electronic monitoring / O. Reg.316/21 with having-and-providing duties and a 25-employee threshold.
